The theory of planned behavior (TPB) is a cognitive theory by Ajzen (1985) that extends the earliertheory of reasoned actionby adding a third predictor, perceived behavioral control.

Ajzen (1985) describes TPB as a cognitive theory that proposes that an individual’s decision to engage in a specific behavior can be predicated by their intention to engage in that behavior.

sections.heading: Key Takeaways
sections.content:
- TPB:Ajzen’s (1985, 1991) theory holds that the best predictor of a behavior is a person’s intention to perform it.

- Three Predictors:intention is shaped by attitude toward the behavior, subjective norms, and perceived behavioral control (PBC).

- PBC:a person’s belief about how easy or difficult a behavior will be; unlike the other two predictors it can also shape behavior directly, without going through intention.

- Intention-Behavior Gap:intention predicts behavior only moderately. Webb and Sheeran (2006) found that experimentally raising intention by a medium-to-large amount produced only a small-to-medium change in behavior.

- Implementation Intentions:specific “if-then” plans (Gollwitzer, 1999) for when, where and how a goal will be acted on are the leading way to close that gap.

- Modern Evidence:recent meta-analyses confirm that interventions targeting TPB’s predictors do change behavior, even though the effect on behavior remains more modest than the effect on intention.

sections.heading: Behavioral intentions
sections.content:
The central premise of the TPB is that human behavior is most proximally and directly determined by a person’s behavioral intentions.

Behavioral intention represents a person’s readiness to perform a given behavior. It acts as a cognitive predisposition: a mental state that precedes the physical act.

This construct indicates how much effort an individual plans to exert. Generally, stronger intentions lead to a higher probability of behavior execution.

According to TPB, intentions are determined by three variables:

sections.heading: 1. Specific Attitudes Toward the Behavior
sections.content:
Attitude toward the behavior constitutes the first major pillar of the TPB framework.

It reflects the degree to which a person has a favorable or unfavorable evaluation of the behavior in question.

This evaluation stems from behavioral beliefs, which are the perceived consequences of an action. For example, a student may believe that studying daily leads to high grades.

If they value high grades, they develop a positive attitude toward studying. Specificity is vital here. General attitudes rarely predict specific actions.

Only attitudes toward a precise behavior at a specific time reliably forecast outcomes.

sections.heading: 2. Subjective norms
sections.content:
Subjective norms represent the second pillar: perceived social pressure.

This reflects how others might view the behavior.

Significant others include influential figures like parents, peers, or medical professionals. These norms arise from normative beliefs, which are expectations attributed to these important groups.

A person also considers their motivation to comply.

This is the internal desire to meet those social expectations.

If a social circle values fitness, an individual feels higher pressure to exercise regularly.

sections.heading: 3. Perceived behavioral control
sections.content:
Perceived Behavioral Control (PBC) refers to an individual’s perception of the ease or difficulty of performing a specific task.

This depends on internal factors, such as our own ability and determination, and external factors, such as the resources and support available.

The theory says perceived control works in two ways. First, it shapes our intentions: the more control we think we have, the stronger our intention to act. Second, it can shape behavior directly, independently of intention, when someone with genuinely high control simply tries harder and longer to succeed.

PBC is conceptually close toself-efficacy. Self-efficacy is the belief in one’s own competence to succeed in a situation.

Ajzen (2002) later clarified that PBC actually combines two distinguishable parts. One is self-efficacy: confidence in one’s ability. The other is controllability, the belief that performance is up to the person rather than blocked by outside circumstances. PBC is broader than self-efficacy alone.

The theory of planned behavior is an extension of thetheory of reasoned action(Ajzen & Fishbein, 1980; Fishbein & Ajzen, 1975).

According to the theory of planned behavior, perceived behavioral control works alongside behavioral intention to predict whether the behavior is actually carried out.

sections.heading: Examples
sections.content: Here are some examples of how the three factors of the Theory of Planned Behavior (TPB) operate in real-world decision-making:

sections.heading: 1. Specific Attitudes Toward the Behavior
sections.content:
This factor involves an individual’s evaluation of a specific action and their beliefs about its consequences.

An individual might hold a positive outcome expectancy, believing that if they give up smoking, they will be healthier, have sweeter breath, save money, and find exercising easier.

They might also have a negative outcome expectancy, such as worrying they will gain weight if they quit.

Their overall attitude is determined by how much they value these specific outcomes, such as concluding, “It is important for me to be healthier”.

A woman’s general attitude toward birth control is a poor predictor of her behavior.

However, her specific attitude towardusing birth control pills during the next two yearsserves as a highly accurate predictor.

A person might weigh the consequences of eating more nutritiously, such as feeling healthier, against negative feelings such as hunger or sugar withdrawal. Weighing these against each other forms their attitude about changing their diet.

sections.heading: 2. Subjective Norms
sections.content:
This factor is driven by the perceived social pressure from significant others and the individual’s motivation to comply with those expectations.

A person named Deepa might have a negative attitude toward classical music and ordinarily wouldn’t attend a violin concert.

However, if her best friend is playing in the concert, Deepa may believe her friend will be highly disappointed and insulted if she doesn’t show up.

This strong subjective norm overrides her personal attitude, making it highly likely she will attend.

A person might hold a negative attitude toward dieting (e.g., “I don’t really like dieting”). They may still form a positive intention to change their eating habits, because all of their friends eat healthily and they want to fit in.

A smoker might feel immense pressure from their family and friends who strongly want them to quit, combined with their own internal motivation to please their loved ones.

sections.heading: 3. Perceived Behavioral Control (PBC)
sections.content:
This refers to a person’s confidence in their ability to overcome barriers and successfully execute the behavior.

If an individual believes it will be easy to avoid smoking even when they go out to a pub in the evening, they have high perceived behavioral control.

Conversely, someone who believes they are completely unable to quit, perhaps due to several failed attempts in the past, has low perceived behavioral control. They likely will not even form an intention to try.

A person might genuinely intend to change their diet because they believe they have the willpower to do it.

However, someone else in their household may actually control the purchasing and preparation of their food. When actual control is this low, the behavioral change is unlikely despite their intentions.

A person will form a strong behavioral intention for a task they perceive as easy, such as remembering to buy milk on the way home from work.

They will form a much weaker intention for a task they perceive as difficult or demanding, such as consistently remembering to use a condom during sexual intercourse.

sections.heading: Health Interventions
sections.content:
Implementation intentions have proven particularly effective in health contexts. They are specific “if-then” plans for exactly when, where and how a goal will be acted on.

Women instructed to form one completed a breast self-examination far more often than those with only a general intention. The implementation-intention group specified exactly when and where they would carry it out (Orbell, Hodgkins, & Sheeran, 1997).

The same principle applies elsewhere too. It has meaningfully enhanced outcomes in weight loss programmes and smoking cessation efforts.

sections.heading: Pro-Environmental Behaviour
sections.content:
Environmental behaviour follows a similar pattern.

In one workplace study, employees wrote down and mentally visualised precisely when, where and how they would recycle their plastic cups. They recycled nearly four times as many cups as a control group with no such plan, a substantial effect from a minimal intervention (Holland, Aarts, & Langendam, 2006).

sections.heading: Civic Engagement
sections.content:
Implementation intentions have also proven effective in voter mobilisation.

Prompting people to articulate a concrete voting plan more than doubled the effectiveness of a mobilisation call (Nickerson & Rogers, 2010). The plan specified what time they would vote, where they would come from, and how they would get to the polling station.

sections.heading: Smoking and Alcohol Use
sections.content:
TPB is the most widely used model in health psychology. It has proven particularly useful in predicting intentions related to smoking and alcohol consumption.

Hagger et al. (2011) found that all three components of the model, personal attitudes, subjective norms, and perceived behavioural control, correlated with alcohol-dependent individuals’ intentions to limit or stop drinking.

Crucially, those intentions also predicted actual behaviour, with the model accurately forecasting the approximate number of units consumed at both one and three months.

Its predictive power did have limits, however. It failed to account for binge drinking episodes.

Evidence for the role of perceived behavioural control comes from Penny (1996). Smokers who had previously failed to quit were less likely to believe they could succeed, and therefore less likely to attempt quitting again.

This illustrates how past experience shapes perceived control, which in turn shapes intention, precisely as TPB predicts.

sections.heading: Automaticity and Resource Conservation
sections.content:
Implementation intentions facilitate “strategic automaticity.” This allows behaviors to occur without conscious deliberation.

Automaticity refers to the ability to perform actions quickly and without intense mental focus. Because the decision is made in advance, the individual avoids the “action initiation” struggle.

They do not need to rely on dwindling reserves of willpower or self-control. The situational cue triggers the behavior directly.

This mechanism bypasses common barriers like forgetfulness, procrastination, or competing distractions.

Consequently, the behavior becomes more resilient to stressful or busy environments.

sections.heading: Critical Evaluation
sections.content: The Theory of Planned Behavior (TPB) is one of the most widely applied social cognition models for understanding deliberative human actions. A critical evaluation reveals real strengths alongside several significant theoretical, methodological, and practical limitations.

sections.heading: Strengths
sections.content:
- Predicts intention well:across many behaviours and cultures, attitude, subjective norms and PBC jointly account for a large share of the variance in intention (Armitage & Conner, 2001).

- PBC earns its place:adding perceived behavioural control improves prediction over the earlier two-component theory of reasoned action and extends the model to behaviours that are not fully voluntary.

- Parsimonious and generative:its clear belief-based structure tells practitioners exactly which beliefs to target, making it highly productive for designing health, environmental and consumer interventions.

- Explicit measurement guidance:the principle of compatibility and Ajzen’s questionnaire guidelines make the model’s constructs measurable and testable.

sections.heading: 1. The Intention-Behavior Gap
sections.content:
One of the most persistent criticisms of the TPB is its failure to consistently predict actual behavior, an issue widely referred to as the “intention-behavior gap”.

This gap describes the failure to translate strong intentions into actual actions.

People often intend to change habits but fail due to distractions or procrastination. To solve this, researchers advocate for implementation intentions.

Webb and Sheeran (2006) provide the clearest experimental test of the gap.

- Aim:to establish whether intention is a genuine cause of behavior, not just something that happens to occur alongside it.

- Method:they pooled 47 experiments that had randomly assigned participants to a manipulation that raised intention, versus a control condition.

- Results:a medium-to-large rise in intention (d = 0.66) produced only a small-to-medium change in behavior (d = 0.36).

- Conclusion:intention is a genuine but only partial cause of behavior, which is why strong intentions so often fail to convert into action.

Aim:to establish whether intention is a genuine cause of behavior, not just something that happens to occur alongside it.

Method:they pooled 47 experiments that had randomly assigned participants to a manipulation that raised intention, versus a control condition.

Results:a medium-to-large rise in intention (d = 0.66) produced only a small-to-medium change in behavior (d = 0.36).

Conclusion:intention is a genuine but only partial cause of behavior, which is why strong intentions so often fail to convert into action.

Implementation intentions close the gap by tying the best-laid plans to concrete situational triggers. This transforms abstract desires into executable, automatic actions.

This shifts intending into acting.

These plans specify exactly when, where, and how a goal will be achieved. They utilize “if-then” logic to link situational cues to specific actions.

One example: exercising every Monday after work. This specific plan makes the behavior more automatic when the trigger occurs.

sections.heading: 2. Over-Reliance on Rationality and Cognitive Variables
sections.content:
The TPB is fundamentally a cognitive model. It derives from expected utility theory and assumes individuals are rational actors who systematically weigh the implications and outcomes of their actions before deciding.

Because it assumes a high degree of voluntary control and rational calculation, the TPB struggles to account for irrational, spontaneous, or emotionally driven decisions.

Critics say it overemphasizesperceivedcognitive variables.

By focusing entirely on an individual’s “perceived” social norms and “perceived” behavioral control, the model overlooks observable social and environmental facts. These facts exert real, objective influence on a person’s behavior regardless of their perception.

sections.heading: 3. Omission of Key Predictive Variables
sections.content:
Because the TPB’s predictive power for actual behavior is notably lower than for intentions, researchers argue that the model is incomplete and needs to incorporate additional variables.

Critical omissions include:

- Past Behavior:The TPB does not adequately consider an individual’s past behavior, despite evidence that past actions are often one of the strongest and most accurate predictors of future behavior.

- Moral Norms:The TPB relies on subjective social norms, but many behaviors are driven by internal moral norms, particularly actions that directly affect others, such as condom use or drink driving.

- Anticipatory Regret:The TPB lacks an emotional dimension. Research shows that anticipating the negative emotions or regret that might follow a decision (or a failure to act) significantly influences future intentions and behaviors.

- Self-Identity:How individuals perceive and label themselves (e.g., viewing oneself as a “green consumer”) can influence their intentions above and beyond the core variables identified in the TPB.

sections.heading: 4. Direction of Causality and Correlational Limitations
sections.content:
The TPB postulates a unidirectional flow: attitudes, subjective norms, and perceived behavioral control shape intentions, which in turn shape behavior.

However, critics point out that the model fails to acknowledge the potential bidirectional transaction between these variables, as actual behavior can reflexively shape and alter a person’s attitudes over time.

Furthermore, the vast majority of research supporting the TPB relies on cross-sectional or correlational data.

Because these studies simply measure the fit of the model against observed data, the direction of causality is ultimately only inferred. Untangling true cause-and-effect relationships requires more prospective, longitudinal studies.

sections.heading: 5. Methodological Vulnerabilities
sections.content:
The methods used to test the TPB have inherent weaknesses.

Studies heavily rely on self-reported data, such as asking participants to report their condom use or dietary habits. This relies on the risky assumption that self-reported behavior accurately reflects actual everyday behavior.

TPB questionnaires are also vulnerable to ordering effects.

Experiments have shown that simply muddling the order of the questions regarding threat, attitude, and normative beliefs significantly alters the intercorrelations between these variables.

This suggests that social desirability and the perceived importance of the topic can artificially inflate the model’s apparent validity.

sections.heading: 6. Lack of Universality and Cultural Bias
sections.content:
Finally, the TPB is a highly generalized model intended to cover all kinds of health and social behaviors. Critics call this a false one-size-fits-all framework.

Different factors are salient for different behaviors. Subjective norms may strongly predict smoking cessation, for example, but say little about vitamin intake.

Moreover, the TPB has mostly been tested in the West. The model’s emphasis on individual autonomy, personal attitudes, and perceived control reflects Western biases. It may not universally apply to interdependent orcollectivist cultures, highlighting the need for a more culturally relative approach to behavioral prediction.

This individualist framing overlaps with what psychologists call cultural bias. Research emphasising personal control and individual reasoning can understate social, structural and economic constraints on behaviour, particularly in collectivist settings.

sections.heading: Contemporary Research
sections.content:
Since the 2014 exchange between critics and Ajzen over whether TPB should be “retired,” the debate has moved from opinion to accumulating meta-analytic evidence.

Steinmetz, Knappstein, Ajzen, Schmidt and Kabst (2016) pooled 123 published interventions from 82 papers that had manipulated TPB’s predictors. They estimated the effect on behavior across all of them.

Interventions produced a medium effect on behavior, about .50. The largest gains came from interventions delivered to public groups rather than private individuals.

This evidence comes from experiments, not correlational surveys, so it directly answers the retirement critique. Changing TPB’s predictors does change behavior, even though behavior remains harder to predict than intention.

Hagger et al. (2022) meta-analyzed 36 prospective health-behavior studies. They found that PBC moderates the intention-behavior link specifically. It does not moderate the earlier links that form the intention itself. Perceived control matters most when acting.

Yang, Li and Liu (2025) tested this directly for exercise, meta-analyzing 92 studies covering over 47,000 participants. Intention predicted exercise behavior only moderately on its own (r = .41).

Planning closes much of that gap.

Adding action planning and coping planning as a chain of mediators raised the variance explained from 28% to 37%. Action control alone accounted for over 13% of the total effect.

Together, these studies point to the same practical lesson. Closing the gap between intending and doing depends less on strengthening intention itself, and more on the planning and follow-through that happens after it.

sections.heading: Interaction of Nature and Nurture
sections.content:
Behavioral intentions result from a continuous interaction between biological endowment and environmental experience.

Psychology rejects the idea that behavior is determined by only one of these forces.

sections.heading: The Role of Nature
sections.content:
Nature provides the baseline physiological hardware for human motivations. Evolutionary adaptations guide certain innate drives, such as the intention to protect kin.

Temperament also influences behavioral style: the biologically based differences in emotional reactivity. These genetic factors establish a range of reaction for an individual’s potential.

sections.heading: The Role of Nurture
sections.content:
Nurture encompasses the social conditioning and learning experiences that shape specific plans. Through socialization, individuals learn the rules and moral codes of their culture.

Social Learning Theory suggests that we form intentions by observing rewarded models. The environment provides that triggering context.

sections.heading: Reciprocal Determinism
sections.content:
The relationship between biology and environment is bidirectional.

Reciprocal determinism suggests that individuals actively influence their surroundings while being shaped by them.

Niche-picking occurs when a person’s genetic traits lead them to seek specific environments. These environments then reinforce the individual’s initial behavioral intentions.

sections.heading: Study 1: Breast Self-Examination (Orbell, Hodgkins, & Sheeran, 1997)
sections.content:
- Aim:To investigate if implementation intentions increase the frequency of breast self-examinations (BSE).

- Procedure:A group of 148 women was recruited for the study. Participants were randomly assigned to either a goal intention group or an implementation intention group. The latter group was asked to state exactly when and where they would perform the BSE.

- Findings:Data showed that 64% of the implementation group performed the BSE. Only 14% of the control group completed the examination.

- Conclusions:Specifying situational parameters significantly enhances the likelihood of following through with health-related behaviors.

sections.heading: Study 2: Pro-Environmental Behavior (Holland, Aarts, & Langendam, 2006)
sections.content:
- Aim:To test if planning can increase recycling behavior in a workplace setting.

- Procedure:Employees at a large organization were studied. One group was required to write down exactly when and how they would recycle their plastic cups. A control group received only general information about the benefits of recycling.

- Findings:The group with specific plans recycled four times as many cups as the control group. This effect remained consistent over several weeks.

- Conclusions:Concrete planning creates a persistent behavioral change that far exceeds the impact of general motivation.

sections.heading: Study 3: Voter Mobilization (Nickerson & Rogers, 2010)
sections.content:
- Aim:To determine if “making a plan” increases voter turnout during a primary election.

- Procedure:Over 280,000 potential voters were contacted via phone. One group was asked standard mobilization questions. Another group was asked specific questions about their timing, location, and transportation to the polls.

- Findings:The “implementation” phone calls were more than twice as effective. Turnout increased significantly among those who articulated a specific plan.

- Conclusions:Strategic questioning that forces implementation planning is a highly effective tool for civic engagement.

sections.heading: How does TPB differ from the Theory of Reasoned Action?
sections.content: The primary difference between the Theory of Planned Behaviour (TPB) and theTheory of Reasoned Action(TRA) is a third component:perceived behavioural control. It was added to address behaviours that are not entirely under an individual’s voluntary control.

sections.heading: Limitations of the Theory of Reasoned Action (TRA)
sections.content:
The TRA, originally developed by Martin Fishbein and Icek Ajzen in the 1970s, assumes that human behaviour is goal-directed and driven by a person’sbehavioural intention.

Under the TRA framework, this intention is shaped by only two factors:

- Attitude towards the behaviour:An individual’s personal evaluation of the behaviour, based on their beliefs about the expected outcomes and consequences.

- Subjective norms:The perceived social pressure from significant others (such as family and friends) regarding whether the behaviour is desirable or acceptable, combined with the individual’s motivation to comply with those expectations.

The central limitation of the TRA is its assumption that individuals are completely rational decision-makers and that their behaviour is entirelyvolitional—meaning it is strictly under their personal control.

Consequently, the TRA is inadequate for explaining situations where an individual strongly intends to perform an action but fails to do so. Environmental obstacles, a lack of resources, or addictive habits can all get in the way.

sections.heading: TPB’s Addition: Perceived Behavioural Control (PBC)
sections.content:
To overcome the TRA’s inability to account for non-volitional behaviours, Ajzen extended the model in 1985 to create the TPB by introducingperceived behavioural control(PBC).

PBC refers to an individual’s belief regarding how easy or difficult it is to successfully perform a specific behaviour, particularly when facing potential barriers.

This extension had deep roots.

Fishbein and Ajzen had studied the attitude-behaviour relationship since the late 1960s. The theory of reasoned action that TPB extended was formalised in 1975.

Ajzen’s 1985 chapterFrom Intentions to Actionsintroduced PBC. The theory reached its mature form in a widely-cited 1991 paper.

This new component is fundamentally linked to Albert Bandura’s concept ofself-efficacy—the belief in one’s capacity to exercise control over events and effectively execute actions.

By adding PBC, the TPB accounts for two critical types of control factors that the TRA ignores:

- Internal control factors:The individual’s personal skills, abilities, and knowledge.

- External control factors:Environmental obstacles, access to resources, and opportunities.

sections.heading: How the TPB Operates Differently
sections.content:
In the TPB framework, PBC interacts with attitudes and subjective norms to determine the strength of a person’s behavioural intention.

If a person believes a task is too difficult or completely outside their control, their intention to act will be weak. This holds regardless of how positive their attitude is or how supportive their social network might be.

PBC works differently from the other two predictors. Unlike attitudes and subjective norms, it can bypass intention entirely to exert adirectinfluence on actual behaviour.

If an individual’s perception of control is accurate, this direct link helps explain why they succeed independently of their initial intentions.

Because the TPB incorporates this measure of personal control, along with past behaviour, it has generally proven more successful than the TRA at predicting complex behaviours. Past behaviour matters because it heavily influences a person’s confidence.

It is especially effective for predicting actions that require overcoming significant challenges, such as quitting smoking, adhering to an exercise regimen, or making dietary changes, where willpower alone is insufficient.

## Key Takeaways

- TPB:Ajzen’s (1985, 1991) theory holds that the best predictor of a behavior is a person’s intention to perform it.

- Three Predictors:intention is shaped by attitude toward the behavior, subjective norms, and perceived behavioral control (PBC).

- PBC:a person’s belief about how easy or difficult a behavior will be; unlike the other two predictors it can also shape behavior directly, without going through intention.

- Intention-Behavior Gap:intention predicts behavior only moderately. Webb and Sheeran (2006) found that experimentally raising intention by a medium-to-large amount produced only a small-to-medium change in behavior.

- Implementation Intentions:specific “if-then” plans (Gollwitzer, 1999) for when, where and how a goal will be acted on are the leading way to close that gap.

- Modern Evidence:recent meta-analyses confirm that interventions targeting TPB’s predictors do change behavior, even though the effect on behavior remains more modest than the effect on intention.

## Behavioral intentions

The central premise of the TPB is that human behavior is most proximally and directly determined by a person’s behavioral intentions.

Behavioral intention represents a person’s readiness to perform a given behavior. It acts as a cognitive predisposition: a mental state that precedes the physical act.

This construct indicates how much effort an individual plans to exert. Generally, stronger intentions lead to a higher probability of behavior execution.

According to TPB, intentions are determined by three variables:

## 1. Specific Attitudes Toward the Behavior

Attitude toward the behavior constitutes the first major pillar of the TPB framework.

It reflects the degree to which a person has a favorable or unfavorable evaluation of the behavior in question.

This evaluation stems from behavioral beliefs, which are the perceived consequences of an action. For example, a student may believe that studying daily leads to high grades.

If they value high grades, they develop a positive attitude toward studying. Specificity is vital here. General attitudes rarely predict specific actions.

Only attitudes toward a precise behavior at a specific time reliably forecast outcomes.

## 2. Subjective norms

Subjective norms represent the second pillar: perceived social pressure.

This reflects how others might view the behavior.

Significant others include influential figures like parents, peers, or medical professionals. These norms arise from normative beliefs, which are expectations attributed to these important groups.

A person also considers their motivation to comply.

This is the internal desire to meet those social expectations.

If a social circle values fitness, an individual feels higher pressure to exercise regularly.

## 3. Perceived behavioral control

Perceived Behavioral Control (PBC) refers to an individual’s perception of the ease or difficulty of performing a specific task.

This depends on internal factors, such as our own ability and determination, and external factors, such as the resources and support available.

The theory says perceived control works in two ways. First, it shapes our intentions: the more control we think we have, the stronger our intention to act. Second, it can shape behavior directly, independently of intention, when someone with genuinely high control simply tries harder and longer to succeed.

PBC is conceptually close toself-efficacy. Self-efficacy is the belief in one’s own competence to succeed in a situation.

Ajzen (2002) later clarified that PBC actually combines two distinguishable parts. One is self-efficacy: confidence in one’s ability. The other is controllability, the belief that performance is up to the person rather than blocked by outside circumstances. PBC is broader than self-efficacy alone.

The theory of planned behavior is an extension of thetheory of reasoned action(Ajzen & Fishbein, 1980; Fishbein & Ajzen, 1975).

According to the theory of planned behavior, perceived behavioral control works alongside behavioral intention to predict whether the behavior is actually carried out.

## Examples

Here are some examples of how the three factors of the Theory of Planned Behavior (TPB) operate in real-world decision-making:

## 1. Specific Attitudes Toward the Behavior

This factor involves an individual’s evaluation of a specific action and their beliefs about its consequences.

An individual might hold a positive outcome expectancy, believing that if they give up smoking, they will be healthier, have sweeter breath, save money, and find exercising easier.

They might also have a negative outcome expectancy, such as worrying they will gain weight if they quit.

Their overall attitude is determined by how much they value these specific outcomes, such as concluding, “It is important for me to be healthier”.

A woman’s general attitude toward birth control is a poor predictor of her behavior.

However, her specific attitude towardusing birth control pills during the next two yearsserves as a highly accurate predictor.

A person might weigh the consequences of eating more nutritiously, such as feeling healthier, against negative feelings such as hunger or sugar withdrawal. Weighing these against each other forms their attitude about changing their diet.

## 2. Subjective Norms

This factor is driven by the perceived social pressure from significant others and the individual’s motivation to comply with those expectations.

A person named Deepa might have a negative attitude toward classical music and ordinarily wouldn’t attend a violin concert.

However, if her best friend is playing in the concert, Deepa may believe her friend will be highly disappointed and insulted if she doesn’t show up.

This strong subjective norm overrides her personal attitude, making it highly likely she will attend.

A person might hold a negative attitude toward dieting (e.g., “I don’t really like dieting”). They may still form a positive intention to change their eating habits, because all of their friends eat healthily and they want to fit in.

A smoker might feel immense pressure from their family and friends who strongly want them to quit, combined with their own internal motivation to please their loved ones.

## 3. Perceived Behavioral Control (PBC)

This refers to a person’s confidence in their ability to overcome barriers and successfully execute the behavior.

If an individual believes it will be easy to avoid smoking even when they go out to a pub in the evening, they have high perceived behavioral control.

Conversely, someone who believes they are completely unable to quit, perhaps due to several failed attempts in the past, has low perceived behavioral control. They likely will not even form an intention to try.

A person might genuinely intend to change their diet because they believe they have the willpower to do it.

However, someone else in their household may actually control the purchasing and preparation of their food. When actual control is this low, the behavioral change is unlikely despite their intentions.

A person will form a strong behavioral intention for a task they perceive as easy, such as remembering to buy milk on the way home from work.

They will form a much weaker intention for a task they perceive as difficult or demanding, such as consistently remembering to use a condom during sexual intercourse.

## Health Interventions

Implementation intentions have proven particularly effective in health contexts. They are specific “if-then” plans for exactly when, where and how a goal will be acted on.

Women instructed to form one completed a breast self-examination far more often than those with only a general intention. The implementation-intention group specified exactly when and where they would carry it out (Orbell, Hodgkins, & Sheeran, 1997).

The same principle applies elsewhere too. It has meaningfully enhanced outcomes in weight loss programmes and smoking cessation efforts.

## Pro-Environmental Behaviour

Environmental behaviour follows a similar pattern.

In one workplace study, employees wrote down and mentally visualised precisely when, where and how they would recycle their plastic cups. They recycled nearly four times as many cups as a control group with no such plan, a substantial effect from a minimal intervention (Holland, Aarts, & Langendam, 2006).

## Civic Engagement

Implementation intentions have also proven effective in voter mobilisation.

Prompting people to articulate a concrete voting plan more than doubled the effectiveness of a mobilisation call (Nickerson & Rogers, 2010). The plan specified what time they would vote, where they would come from, and how they would get to the polling station.

## Smoking and Alcohol Use

TPB is the most widely used model in health psychology. It has proven particularly useful in predicting intentions related to smoking and alcohol consumption.

Hagger et al. (2011) found that all three components of the model, personal attitudes, subjective norms, and perceived behavioural control, correlated with alcohol-dependent individuals’ intentions to limit or stop drinking.

Crucially, those intentions also predicted actual behaviour, with the model accurately forecasting the approximate number of units consumed at both one and three months.

Its predictive power did have limits, however. It failed to account for binge drinking episodes.

Evidence for the role of perceived behavioural control comes from Penny (1996). Smokers who had previously failed to quit were less likely to believe they could succeed, and therefore less likely to attempt quitting again.

This illustrates how past experience shapes perceived control, which in turn shapes intention, precisely as TPB predicts.

## Automaticity and Resource Conservation

Implementation intentions facilitate “strategic automaticity.” This allows behaviors to occur without conscious deliberation.

Automaticity refers to the ability to perform actions quickly and without intense mental focus. Because the decision is made in advance, the individual avoids the “action initiation” struggle.

They do not need to rely on dwindling reserves of willpower or self-control. The situational cue triggers the behavior directly.

This mechanism bypasses common barriers like forgetfulness, procrastination, or competing distractions.

Consequently, the behavior becomes more resilient to stressful or busy environments.

## Critical Evaluation

The Theory of Planned Behavior (TPB) is one of the most widely applied social cognition models for understanding deliberative human actions. A critical evaluation reveals real strengths alongside several significant theoretical, methodological, and practical limitations.

## Strengths

- Predicts intention well:across many behaviours and cultures, attitude, subjective norms and PBC jointly account for a large share of the variance in intention (Armitage & Conner, 2001).

- PBC earns its place:adding perceived behavioural control improves prediction over the earlier two-component theory of reasoned action and extends the model to behaviours that are not fully voluntary.

- Parsimonious and generative:its clear belief-based structure tells practitioners exactly which beliefs to target, making it highly productive for designing health, environmental and consumer interventions.

- Explicit measurement guidance:the principle of compatibility and Ajzen’s questionnaire guidelines make the model’s constructs measurable and testable.

## 1. The Intention-Behavior Gap

One of the most persistent criticisms of the TPB is its failure to consistently predict actual behavior, an issue widely referred to as the “intention-behavior gap”.

This gap describes the failure to translate strong intentions into actual actions.

People often intend to change habits but fail due to distractions or procrastination. To solve this, researchers advocate for implementation intentions.

Webb and Sheeran (2006) provide the clearest experimental test of the gap.

- Aim:to establish whether intention is a genuine cause of behavior, not just something that happens to occur alongside it.

- Method:they pooled 47 experiments that had randomly assigned participants to a manipulation that raised intention, versus a control condition.

- Results:a medium-to-large rise in intention (d = 0.66) produced only a small-to-medium change in behavior (d = 0.36).

- Conclusion:intention is a genuine but only partial cause of behavior, which is why strong intentions so often fail to convert into action.

Implementation intentions close the gap by tying the best-laid plans to concrete situational triggers. This transforms abstract desires into executable, automatic actions.

This shifts intending into acting.

These plans specify exactly when, where, and how a goal will be achieved. They utilize “if-then” logic to link situational cues to specific actions.

One example: exercising every Monday after work. This specific plan makes the behavior more automatic when the trigger occurs.

## 2. Over-Reliance on Rationality and Cognitive Variables

The TPB is fundamentally a cognitive model. It derives from expected utility theory and assumes individuals are rational actors who systematically weigh the implications and outcomes of their actions before deciding.

Because it assumes a high degree of voluntary control and rational calculation, the TPB struggles to account for irrational, spontaneous, or emotionally driven decisions.

Critics say it overemphasizesperceivedcognitive variables.

By focusing entirely on an individual’s “perceived” social norms and “perceived” behavioral control, the model overlooks observable social and environmental facts. These facts exert real, objective influence on a person’s behavior regardless of their perception.

## 3. Omission of Key Predictive Variables

Because the TPB’s predictive power for actual behavior is notably lower than for intentions, researchers argue that the model is incomplete and needs to incorporate additional variables.

Critical omissions include:

- Past Behavior:The TPB does not adequately consider an individual’s past behavior, despite evidence that past actions are often one of the strongest and most accurate predictors of future behavior.

- Moral Norms:The TPB relies on subjective social norms, but many behaviors are driven by internal moral norms, particularly actions that directly affect others, such as condom use or drink driving.

- Anticipatory Regret:The TPB lacks an emotional dimension. Research shows that anticipating the negative emotions or regret that might follow a decision (or a failure to act) significantly influences future intentions and behaviors.

- Self-Identity:How individuals perceive and label themselves (e.g., viewing oneself as a “green consumer”) can influence their intentions above and beyond the core variables identified in the TPB.

## 4. Direction of Causality and Correlational Limitations

The TPB postulates a unidirectional flow: attitudes, subjective norms, and perceived behavioral control shape intentions, which in turn shape behavior.

However, critics point out that the model fails to acknowledge the potential bidirectional transaction between these variables, as actual behavior can reflexively shape and alter a person’s attitudes over time.

Furthermore, the vast majority of research supporting the TPB relies on cross-sectional or correlational data.

Because these studies simply measure the fit of the model against observed data, the direction of causality is ultimately only inferred. Untangling true cause-and-effect relationships requires more prospective, longitudinal studies.

## 5. Methodological Vulnerabilities

The methods used to test the TPB have inherent weaknesses.

Studies heavily rely on self-reported data, such as asking participants to report their condom use or dietary habits. This relies on the risky assumption that self-reported behavior accurately reflects actual everyday behavior.

TPB questionnaires are also vulnerable to ordering effects.

Experiments have shown that simply muddling the order of the questions regarding threat, attitude, and normative beliefs significantly alters the intercorrelations between these variables.

This suggests that social desirability and the perceived importance of the topic can artificially inflate the model’s apparent validity.

## 6. Lack of Universality and Cultural Bias

Finally, the TPB is a highly generalized model intended to cover all kinds of health and social behaviors. Critics call this a false one-size-fits-all framework.

Different factors are salient for different behaviors. Subjective norms may strongly predict smoking cessation, for example, but say little about vitamin intake.

Moreover, the TPB has mostly been tested in the West. The model’s emphasis on individual autonomy, personal attitudes, and perceived control reflects Western biases. It may not universally apply to interdependent orcollectivist cultures, highlighting the need for a more culturally relative approach to behavioral prediction.

This individualist framing overlaps with what psychologists call cultural bias. Research emphasising personal control and individual reasoning can understate social, structural and economic constraints on behaviour, particularly in collectivist settings.

## Contemporary Research

Since the 2014 exchange between critics and Ajzen over whether TPB should be “retired,” the debate has moved from opinion to accumulating meta-analytic evidence.

Steinmetz, Knappstein, Ajzen, Schmidt and Kabst (2016) pooled 123 published interventions from 82 papers that had manipulated TPB’s predictors. They estimated the effect on behavior across all of them.

Interventions produced a medium effect on behavior, about .50. The largest gains came from interventions delivered to public groups rather than private individuals.

This evidence comes from experiments, not correlational surveys, so it directly answers the retirement critique. Changing TPB’s predictors does change behavior, even though behavior remains harder to predict than intention.

Hagger et al. (2022) meta-analyzed 36 prospective health-behavior studies. They found that PBC moderates the intention-behavior link specifically. It does not moderate the earlier links that form the intention itself. Perceived control matters most when acting.

Yang, Li and Liu (2025) tested this directly for exercise, meta-analyzing 92 studies covering over 47,000 participants. Intention predicted exercise behavior only moderately on its own (r = .41).

Planning closes much of that gap.

Adding action planning and coping planning as a chain of mediators raised the variance explained from 28% to 37%. Action control alone accounted for over 13% of the total effect.

Together, these studies point to the same practical lesson. Closing the gap between intending and doing depends less on strengthening intention itself, and more on the planning and follow-through that happens after it.

## Interaction of Nature and Nurture

Behavioral intentions result from a continuous interaction between biological endowment and environmental experience.

Psychology rejects the idea that behavior is determined by only one of these forces.

## The Role of Nature

Nature provides the baseline physiological hardware for human motivations. Evolutionary adaptations guide certain innate drives, such as the intention to protect kin.

Temperament also influences behavioral style: the biologically based differences in emotional reactivity. These genetic factors establish a range of reaction for an individual’s potential.

## The Role of Nurture

Nurture encompasses the social conditioning and learning experiences that shape specific plans. Through socialization, individuals learn the rules and moral codes of their culture.

Social Learning Theory suggests that we form intentions by observing rewarded models. The environment provides that triggering context.

## Reciprocal Determinism

The relationship between biology and environment is bidirectional.

Reciprocal determinism suggests that individuals actively influence their surroundings while being shaped by them.

Niche-picking occurs when a person’s genetic traits lead them to seek specific environments. These environments then reinforce the individual’s initial behavioral intentions.

## Study 1: Breast Self-Examination (Orbell, Hodgkins, & Sheeran, 1997)

- Aim:To investigate if implementation intentions increase the frequency of breast self-examinations (BSE).

- Procedure:A group of 148 women was recruited for the study. Participants were randomly assigned to either a goal intention group or an implementation intention group. The latter group was asked to state exactly when and where they would perform the BSE.

- Findings:Data showed that 64% of the implementation group performed the BSE. Only 14% of the control group completed the examination.

- Conclusions:Specifying situational parameters significantly enhances the likelihood of following through with health-related behaviors.

## Study 2: Pro-Environmental Behavior (Holland, Aarts, & Langendam, 2006)

- Aim:To test if planning can increase recycling behavior in a workplace setting.

- Procedure:Employees at a large organization were studied. One group was required to write down exactly when and how they would recycle their plastic cups. A control group received only general information about the benefits of recycling.

- Findings:The group with specific plans recycled four times as many cups as the control group. This effect remained consistent over several weeks.

- Conclusions:Concrete planning creates a persistent behavioral change that far exceeds the impact of general motivation.

## Study 3: Voter Mobilization (Nickerson & Rogers, 2010)

- Aim:To determine if “making a plan” increases voter turnout during a primary election.

- Procedure:Over 280,000 potential voters were contacted via phone. One group was asked standard mobilization questions. Another group was asked specific questions about their timing, location, and transportation to the polls.

- Findings:The “implementation” phone calls were more than twice as effective. Turnout increased significantly among those who articulated a specific plan.

- Conclusions:Strategic questioning that forces implementation planning is a highly effective tool for civic engagement.

## How does TPB differ from the Theory of Reasoned Action?

The primary difference between the Theory of Planned Behaviour (TPB) and theTheory of Reasoned Action(TRA) is a third component:perceived behavioural control. It was added to address behaviours that are not entirely under an individual’s voluntary control.

## Limitations of the Theory of Reasoned Action (TRA)

The TRA, originally developed by Martin Fishbein and Icek Ajzen in the 1970s, assumes that human behaviour is goal-directed and driven by a person’sbehavioural intention.

Under the TRA framework, this intention is shaped by only two factors:

- Attitude towards the behaviour:An individual’s personal evaluation of the behaviour, based on their beliefs about the expected outcomes and consequences.

- Subjective norms:The perceived social pressure from significant others (such as family and friends) regarding whether the behaviour is desirable or acceptable, combined with the individual’s motivation to comply with those expectations.

The central limitation of the TRA is its assumption that individuals are completely rational decision-makers and that their behaviour is entirelyvolitional—meaning it is strictly under their personal control.

Consequently, the TRA is inadequate for explaining situations where an individual strongly intends to perform an action but fails to do so. Environmental obstacles, a lack of resources, or addictive habits can all get in the way.

## TPB’s Addition: Perceived Behavioural Control (PBC)

To overcome the TRA’s inability to account for non-volitional behaviours, Ajzen extended the model in 1985 to create the TPB by introducingperceived behavioural control(PBC).

PBC refers to an individual’s belief regarding how easy or difficult it is to successfully perform a specific behaviour, particularly when facing potential barriers.

This extension had deep roots.

Fishbein and Ajzen had studied the attitude-behaviour relationship since the late 1960s. The theory of reasoned action that TPB extended was formalised in 1975.

Ajzen’s 1985 chapterFrom Intentions to Actionsintroduced PBC. The theory reached its mature form in a widely-cited 1991 paper.

This new component is fundamentally linked to Albert Bandura’s concept ofself-efficacy—the belief in one’s capacity to exercise control over events and effectively execute actions.

By adding PBC, the TPB accounts for two critical types of control factors that the TRA ignores:

- Internal control factors:The individual’s personal skills, abilities, and knowledge.

- External control factors:Environmental obstacles, access to resources, and opportunities.

## How the TPB Operates Differently

In the TPB framework, PBC interacts with attitudes and subjective norms to determine the strength of a person’s behavioural intention.

If a person believes a task is too difficult or completely outside their control, their intention to act will be weak. This holds regardless of how positive their attitude is or how supportive their social network might be.

PBC works differently from the other two predictors. Unlike attitudes and subjective norms, it can bypass intention entirely to exert adirectinfluence on actual behaviour.

If an individual’s perception of control is accurate, this direct link helps explain why they succeed independently of their initial intentions.

Because the TPB incorporates this measure of personal control, along with past behaviour, it has generally proven more successful than the TRA at predicting complex behaviours. Past behaviour matters because it heavily influences a person’s confidence.

It is especially effective for predicting actions that require overcoming significant challenges, such as quitting smoking, adhering to an exercise regimen, or making dietary changes, where willpower alone is insufficient.
